extracted.intended_audience: aspiring fiction writers and early-career authors seeking publication and representation
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, experience-based guidance on writing, finishing manuscripts, querying agents, setting up a writing routine, and avoiding common pitfalls in seeking publication. Targets fiction writers preparing short stories and novels for submission and representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Query letter: literate, well-spoken tone
rubrics_metrics.description: The letter he sent around was literate and well-spoken ("It took four drafts and two arguments with my wife to get that casual tone just right").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft and revise query letters until they achieve a natural, readable, 'casual' but literate tone; invest time (multiple drafts) to get voice right. Example: Frank revised his query four times to obtain the right casual tone. Include clear contact information (address and telephone number) so agents can call.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include publishing credentials when querying
rubrics_metrics.description: Be able to supply an actual list of published short stories, even if they didn’t bring big money, and note reputable magazines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A track record of publication in reputable magazines strengthens queries. Listing prior short-story publications signals seriousness and can attract agent interest; a prizewinner entry can be particularly helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mention awards/prizes (when applicable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Third, there was the prize-winner. Frank thinks that may have been key.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have won a writing prize or award, highlight it in submissions/queries — it can substantially increase agent interest (it didn’t hurt Frank).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be ready to send requested materials (specific lengths)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several agents asked to see the prizewinning story about the hunter lost in the woods; half a dozen asked to see the first eighty pages of his novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have clean, submission-ready material available (complete stories and at least the opening ~80 pages of a novel) to send promptly when requested. Know what you will send in response to an agent’s request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vet agents by asking for bona fides
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask agents for a list of their bona fides — not a list of clients, but the publishers to whom the agent had sold books and the magazines to which he had sold short stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request verifiable evidence of an agent’s track record (publishers/magazines sold to) to avoid being conned by someone posing as an agent. Don’t accept vague claims — check the agent’s sales history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of agents who charge reading fees
rubrics_metrics.description: You should be especially wary of agents who promise to read your work for a fee. A few such agents are reputable... but all too many are unscrupulous fucks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat paying an agent to read your work as a red flag unless the agency is a well-known exception. Consider that many pay-to-read agents are unscrupulous; seek reputable alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of vanity/for-pay publishing and unscrupulous agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone with a few hundred dollars to invest can place an ad ... calling himself or herself a literary agent ... If you’re that anxious to get published, you might skip agent-hunting or query-letters to publishers and go directly to a vanity press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the risk that some 'agents' are just paid advertisers; if your goal is immediate self-validation and you're unwilling to wait, a vanity press will at least give you a product — but it is not the same as legitimate publication. Prefer legitimate agents and publishers when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for joy, not money
rubrics_metrics.description: Do you do it for the money? The answer is no. I have written because it fulfilled me... I did it for the pure joy of the thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt intrinsic motivation: writing for personal fulfillment and the joy of craft sustains long-term practice and career longevity better than writing primarily for commercial gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use writing as recovery and personal sustenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing is not life, but I think that sometimes it can be a way back to life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn to writing as a method of emotional recovery or reconnection after trauma or loss; it can provide meaning and routine during difficult times (King restarted work during recovery and it helped him regain purpose).

rubrics_metrics.name: Start — the scariest moment is before you start
rubrics_metrics.description: The scariest moment is always just before you start.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overcome inertia by simply beginning; initial sessions may be small and painful, but momentum comes with repetition. King’s first session back lasted 1 hour 40 minutes and he then built up from there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persist through bad drafts and physical difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: All my old tricks seemed to have deserted me... There was no inspiration that first afternoon, only a kind of stubborn determination and the hope that things would get better if I kept at it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect early drafts to be difficult; persistence and steady effort produce improvement. Don’t wait for inspiration — keep working even when it feels like a slog.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange a practical, comfortable workspace
rubrics_metrics.description: Tabby rigged a table in the back hall: 'plenty of plug-ins—you can have your Mac, the little printer, and a fan.' Standing on the corner of the desk was a framed picture... pens, reference materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up a dedicated, ergonomically suitable writing station with required equipment (computer, printer, lamp, fan/ventilation, reference materials) and small personal items that help focus. Adapt workspace to physical limitations (wheelchair-accessible, nearby plugs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the book be the boss
rubrics_metrics.description: Kirby McCauley... used to quote Alfred Bester: 'The book is the boss.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make decisions in service of the work — the needs of the book should guide revisions and choices, not external agendas or vanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust instinct but study mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of it turned out to be dull and most of the rest... has more to do with instinct than with anything resembling 'higher thought.' I found the act of articulating those instinctive truths painfully difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance instinctive feel for language with conscious study of craft (dialogue, character, language mechanics). Be prepared to translate instinct into teachable, repeatable technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid lazy phrasing and near-clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: Although 'dark as a cave' isn’t all that riveting; certainly we’ve heard it before. It is... a bit lazy, not quite a cliché but certainly in the neighborhood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for worn or lazy phrases and rework them to be fresher and more specific. Avoid relying on common shorthand imagery that flattens prose.
